newsitem.title: USA: One buyer takes 15 of Diana's dresses.
newsitem.headline: One buyer takes 15 of Diana's dresses.

text.p: The new owners of Princess Diana's dresses packed Christie's auction house on Thursday to pick up their expensive new gowns, with some even holding them up to full-length mirrors to see if they would fit.
Diana sent a fulsome fax of thanks to Christie's chairman Lord Hindlip for presiding over the charity sale of 79 of her cast-off gowns that fetched more than $3.2 million.

Hindlip, in an interview with Reuters, said that one woman, the chief executive officer of a chain of boutiques in Florida, bought 15 of the dresses including the night's most expensive garment, a gown Diana wore to a dinner at the Reagan White House in which she danced with John Travalta.

He said that the woman asked to remain anonymous but he was certain she would reveal her identity soon. When the sale ended on Wednesday night, Hindlip told reporters the dress was bought by a man whom he described as a great fan of the princess.
"I was wrong," he said, adding, "it was a woman, but she is a great admirer of Princess Diana."
He said Diana sent him a fax on Thursday morning describing her absolute delight that the sale went so well.

The blue silk velvet dress Princess Diana wore for the state dinner hosted by President Ronald Reagan sold for $222,500, a record auction price for a costume. Ironically it surpassed the previous record of $145,000 paid for the costume Travolta wore in the hit film "Saturday Night Fever".

The 79 dresses that the princess wore to such far-flung places as Japan, Pakistan and South Korea during her 15-year-marriage to Britain's Prince Charles were eagerly snapped up as a crowd of 1,100 people at Christie's clapped, cheered, and whistled.

But the 35-year-old princess, whose fairy-tale marriage ended in bitter separation and divorce, slept through it all, oblivious to the spirited bidding by people ranging from women who wished they were her to companies and museums seeking an association with her name and fame.
Hindlip said most of the dresses were bought by companies such as the Romance cable television channel, Britain's Daily Mirror newspaper and other publications, stores and museums.
But several were also bought by women who hope to wear the gowns themselves.
